title: Design a stack that supports push, pop, top, and retrieving the minimum element, all in constant time.
shortTitle: Min Stack: design with O(1) getMin (auxiliary min stack)
keyPoints: Keep a second auxiliary stack whose top always holds the current minimum of the main stack.
On push, push the value to main and push min(value, current min) to the auxiliary stack.
On pop, pop both stacks together so the minimum stays correct as elements are removed.
getMin() is a single peek on the auxiliary stack, giving O(1) time.
Space optimization: push to min stack only when value is less than or equal to current min.
Use BigDecimal and compareTo for banking money comparisons instead of primitive operators.

s1_definition.oneliner: Keep a parallel min stack whose top always holds the minimum of everything currently in the main stack.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Min Stack** – a data-structure design problem that augments a normal stack with O(1) minimum retrieval.
- **Two-stack approach** – maintain a main stack for values and an auxiliary stack where each entry records the minimum of all elements present up to that level.
- **Push rule** – push the value onto the main stack and push `min(value, currentMin)` onto the auxiliary stack.
- **Pop rule** – pop both stacks together so they stay aligned and the minimum stays correct.
- **getMin** – peek the auxiliary stack in O(1); no scanning needed.
- **Space trade-off** – O(n) extra space for the auxiliary stack; an optimization pushes only new minimums.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh at the National Bank of India tracks account balances on a pile of slips. On top of each slip he also writes the lowest balance the account has ever had up to that point. When he removes the top slip, the lowest-ever note on the new top is still correct because it was recorded for that earlier state. At any instant he can glance at the top and know both the current balance and the lowest balance, without rereading the whole pile.

sections.s6_takeaway:
A Min Stack augments a normal stack with an O(1) getMin operation by keeping a second auxiliary stack whose top always holds the current minimum. On every push, I push the value onto the main stack and push the smaller of the new value and the current minimum onto the auxiliary stack. On every pop, I pop both stacks together so the minimum stays correct as elements are removed. The getMin operation is a single peek on the auxiliary stack.

The elegance is in the invariant: at every level, the auxiliary stack entry is the smallest value among all elements from the bottom up to that level. Because the stacks are popped in lockstep, removing the top value also removes its minimum record, and the new top of the auxiliary stack is automatically the correct minimum for whatever remains.

For banking money, I use `BigDecimal` rather than primitives and compare with `compareTo` instead of the `<` operator, because money comparisons must respect scale and precision. There is a space-optimized variant that pushes to the min stack only when a value is less than or equal to the current minimum, but the key detail is using less-than-or-equal rather than strict less-than so that duplicate minimums are tracked correctly.

In my project at the National Bank of India, I used this inside a risk monitor that tracks a customer's intraday balance as positions open and close. The desk constantly asks for the lowest balance to check overdraft thresholds, and the auxiliary min stack answers that in O(1) even as balances churn rapidly. When a position is reversed, popping both stacks immediately surfaces the correct previous minimum without any rescan.

Remember one sentence: keep a parallel min stack in lockstep with the main stack so the top of the min stack is always the current minimum in O(1).
